editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.p: The following history testimony was transcribed from an audiotaped interview with Robert M. Martin conducted by Tom Swope on June 10, 2001 on behalf of the Veterans' Oral History Project. The interview took place in Chagrin Falls, Ohio, and is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.
The interview was transcribed and edited by M. Kate Miller on July 26, 2003.

The reader should bear in mind that he/she is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. This transcript is meant to represent the spoken word; thus, it should be read as a personal memoir and not as a researched monograph or an edited account.

To the extent possible, spellings have been verified by reference resources. In the event that there is uncertainty regarding the spelling of any word contained in this transcript, the demarcation of (ph) will follow to indicate that such word has been spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Question: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Robert M. Martin . Mr. Martin was in the United States Army Air Corps, 15th Air Force, 97th Bomb Group. Mr. Martin served in the European theater, and his highest rank during World War II was first lieutenant. I'm Tom Swope. We recorded this at Mr. Martin's home in Chagrin Falls, Ohio on June 10th, 2001. Bob's age at the time was 82.

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: Answer: I enlisted in August of 1942 in the Air Force cadet program, and the first thing that I had to do was go to Youngstown University from Warren, where I lived at that time, two days of psychology testing and multiple choice reasoning and that sort of thing, and when I got through those two days of testing and the results were forwarded, I think, up to Cleveland, then I came to Cleveland two separate days for physical, and there everything was checked, including parallel vision, and if you didn't have it, you were given the choice of service -- corrective surgery or you wouldn't be accepted in the cadets. And after that spell, which took place in the fall, I finally was called to active duty in February of the next year, 1943, and left from Warren by train for Columbus. And there I had my first issue of army uniform, because we were still considered army, and some more physicals and some more psychological interviews, and when there were enough people there who were being interviewed, a train-load was formed and we took off for San Antonio, Texas. And this was a train made up of old-fashioned coaches, there were no sleepers, and we had a full compliment of people in each car so some of the seats could be folded flat for beds. And some of us, we would flip to see who was gonna sleep on one of the seats and if you lost you got up on the baggage rack, which was overhead in the -- and luckily those were made of parallel steel rods and you could put your belt underneath those and then back through your trouser loops so that you were tied in, because it was a good chance of you bouncing out on the trip. And the trip took three days, actually, to get to San Antone and it was quite an experience, eating in a railroad freight car, which they put up -- they knew the trip would be longer than what we could go without food, but they didn't make any kind of a canteen or anything. It was just a freight car with the stoves and the hotplates or whatever, and we'd go through single file and get to the end and turn around and come back to the coach. And then when we got to San Antonio we were unloaded and sorted out for more physicals and eventually got into squadrons. At that time Hank Greenburgh, who had retired from the -- pro baseball, was athletic director of the whole place and our exercises consisted of all kinds of calisthenics plus wall climbing, and the toughest thing was a crosscountry up and down route, sort of like a steeple chase kind of thing. And we were warned that it was best not to fall down and break anything or you would be pushed back another class, and I did have at one time an ankle sprain, and when I went in to the medics they said, "Well, for something like this we can keep you going if you want to stay with your people," and I said, "What is it?" and so they filled that whole foot and ankle with novocain and I never missed a calisthenic class and it never wore off until about four days, actually, there was that much novocain in there. And so I was able to stay with the class that I was at and from there we went to bombadeer school, and I think that was in Bonham, Texas, and I remember that we spent one Thanksgiving in tents out in the open somewhere and it was a cold, rainy Thanksgiving, but we did have a hot turkey meal, even though it was outside. And the training program for cadets for the -- for all three, navigators and pilots and bombadeers, was a pretty exciting kind of adventure. One of the things that we did was ride in the open back of a small pickup truck with a shotgun through a kind of a crazy route, and every once in a while there would be ground fire, pseudo ground fire, at you, coming out of hidden places, and you had to react while you were standing up in the back of this truck going about 20 mile an hour and shoot back at the targets. And we had -- as green cadets we were under the control of upperclassmen, which were -- they were far more active in the keeping track of our behavior. And they were free to give us all kinds of punishment, and their favorite punishment was walking the compound with a full uniform, and if you had to walk for three or four hours, that depended on how serious the problem was, and it didn't take long to remember or appreciate that that was a real drag to have to do that. Anyway, we eventually did graduate from bombadeer school and got our wings and then we went to Laredo for aerial gunnery, and that was two men to a plane plus the pilot and the instructors, and we would be firing guns at a target, towed, and some of the bombadeer training itself was held inside of hangers on a four-wheel battery-operated or electrically-operated platform, which itself was about ten or twelve feet high and, I would guess, maybe seven or eight feet square, and on it would be a bomb site and an instructor and two cadets. And we had moving targets on the floor of the hanger, which were electronically controlled, and they would have a bullseye target on the top of them. And we would operate this moving platform through the bomb site, and when you got to bombs away you hopefully were over the bull's-eye, and there was an ink dauber that came down and marked the target where you were. So we had hours and hours of that kind of training on the site before we ever got into the air and it was -- I think it was a very good system because we all developed the ability to use the site, and the site itself was -- in those days was a real miracle of precision and you had to be -- well, at that point before we got overseas, we were told that we would be in charge of defending that, and each mission completed you would take the site out of the plane in a carrying kit and it would be registered and safely kept until it was needed for the next mission. Well, that was great in theory but it didn't work overseas. It was just too much hassle and -- just to keep the planes in repair after a mission. And I had -- I guess I didn't show you that -- I had a cigarette lighter made on which I used a phillips screwdriver to keep track of my missions, and I had 46 indentations on that lighter when we went on this last mission and I hadn't put down the previous two. The mission that we got shot down on was my 49th mission, I think, either 48th or 49th, so it was close to time to come back home. And we were carrying thousand-pound bombs and had two majors as pilots, and it was the first time I'd ever flown with a major, and it turned out that we were leading the 97th bomb group and most of the 15th Air Force to the target, which was Augsburg, and there was a ball bearing factory there and a huge marshalling art also. Augsberg was an industrial city of quite a few thousand people, probably several hundred thousand, and a real top-flight European city. And we got hit on the bomb run on the way in, but I stayed on the site and we did drop our bombs. We dropped three of the four and our -- part of our electrical system got shot out, and we had one 1,000-pound bomb hung up and the engineer and I worked for about 15 to 20 minutes trying to, in slang, kick it loose and it just -- it was locked up because the system had been shot out, and it turned out that our headphones -- the navigator and myself had lost communication. And sometime after we had given up on kicking this bomb out, the navigator eased back to the cockpit through the little hole in the floor to see how we were doing because we had a run-away propeller on the left-hand side and an engine on fire on the right-hand side. And on the flight, after we found out that we couldn't get rid of this bomb, the rest of the crew was salvaging stuff out the window and out the bomb bay to strip as much weight as possible off the plane. And, anyway, when the navigator came back from his squatting up through this hole he said, "There isn't anybody up there." He said, "You and I are the only ones here on the plane." They had put it on automatic pilot and everybody had been warned, but nobody knew, as we didn't, that our communications were shot out along with whatever system, you know, so we were there high and dry all by ourselves. It didn't take us long to get out. And I had put in for -- when I started to fly as a lead bombadeer, I had put in for a pilot's chute, which is a backpack, and the other chutes would clip on your chest and there was no way you could have it there and work on the bomb site if you were flying as a lead, so after, I think, 15 missions or so when I started to fly regularly, I was able to get a pilot's backpack and that was much better. I could wear it on the bomb run and still get down over the site. In dropping out of the nose hatch there, one of the straps caught on a rivet and I had to pull myself back up and get loose and drop again, (laughing), so this was a two-stage drop. And the kids in the school room, they got a real hoot out of that, that I had to jump twice in order to get out of the plane.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: As lead bombardier, what specifically was your job?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Well, you're up the whole night before because you had to wait for the target to come in from the -- Rome, which was air force headquarters, and you would prepare target photographs and with a grease pencil indicate the heading on a celluloid overlay as to how you were to go in to the target, and also the altitude would be information that the pilots had, but you had to make sure that the altitude was flown because everything that you put into the site by way of data depended on the exact altitude. And on the trip from takeoff to target you were constantly monitoring the air temperature in increments as you climbed to the bombing altitude and you would come up with a mean temperature. And you did the same thing with the site to figure out, by use of the E6P computer, what the ground wind conditions were, because that was another thing that had to be accounted for in setting up the site so that if you were flying to a target such as that and you had a cross wind, you might have to be anchored into that wind because you were going to drift one way or the other depending on where the wind source was. So you had a busy time, actually, getting up to -- and you had to have all of this done by the time you got to the rallying point, which was before the I.P., or the initial part of the bomb run. And you had constant communication with the navigator and the pilots as to what you were doing. And once we got to the I.P., then the plane was turned over to the bomb site and the bombadeer and the two pilots' responsibility was to stay on the heading and stay at the same air speed and stay at the same altitude. You had to have a constant made up of those various factors in order for the bomb site to be as accurate as it could be, and it was a marvelous creation and you could really -- well, figuratively they talked about putting a bomb in a barrel, but you didn't have to do that. If you got within 50 to 100 feet of a targeted building or a targeted railroad crossing or a bridge, since your bombs were going to drop first and you had wing men on either side and behind you, you were bound to have a pattern which would eliminate that target or damage it to the point that the gig was a success. And I think the worst -- probably the worst missions that I flew were to Ploesti (ph) -- I went there twice -- and another bad target, because of the length of the mission, was a place called Blechammer, and I don't know what the target was at this point, but Blechammer was a real nightmare mission. And those missions to Ploesti and Blechammer and other areas in Czechoslovakia and Poland would last, from takeoff to landing, close to 11 hours. We'd get off before sunrise. You'd be at the plane by 4:30 in the morning, and if you were lead crew you were up all night getting everything ready. The navigator has to see that all of the navigation data was consistent and disbursed to every navigator in the group. And, of course, the pilots had to know what their rallying point was, where all of the various squadrons in a group would meet short of the initial point of the bomb run. And so you -- you had a navigation problem in that you had to -- regardless of weather conditions, you had to make allowances for your flying conditions in order to get to that rallying point because the success of our raids depended on having a multiple number of planes, and we rarely ran into any defensive fire except from the ground. At that point, I don't ever remember, except in immediate target area, that we had to contend with fighters, defense fighters. At the target area they were present and also when we left the target area after bombs away the first thing they did was the pilots would "dump the sticks," which was drop the nose of the plane and give it all the RPM it would go and you'd head off normally to the southwest from any target in Germany in a steady, shallow dive, you know, as fast as you could get out of there. And that would last anywhere from -- oh, I suppose 20 minutes to maybe two hours, depending how deep into Europe we got, but the trip home would be maybe four hours while the trip out was seven hours. And it all depended, you know, on the success. I did lose a roommate on another mission when I was flying as a lead and he was in the right-hand plane, actually, as the secondary lead bombadeer and they took a direct hit and just pulverized in a big ball of fire. But one thing that was an advantage to our planes was the fact that none of our bombs were armed until they were considerably below the airplane. There was a -- what was called an arming wire, which was part of the bomb racks, and a little air screw that fit on the nose of each bomb, and the arming wire would go through to stop that propeller from turning, and as the bombs dropped out of the bay, the wires would slip through and then these little air screws would start to revolve and that would determine how far below the plane the bomb would be armed. So we never had a problem, like the British planes did, of taking off with a load that was already armed. It was a great invention and certainly cut down our casualties. And in the case where you had to come back home with something still hung up in the bomb rack, we simply checked to make certain that the arming wire was in there and -- because if the arming wire was out and the bomb bay was open you would get some air wash that would revolve those little propellers, and if it was enough, I suppose you could probably arm a bomb. So the first thing you had to do with any load that did hang up for any reason or if the -- if your bomb run was cancelled, you had to make certain that the arming wires were all back in -- which was a dumb notation; they were de-arming wires, actually. (laughing) Q: And what made those two missions particularly bad? A: Well, Ploesti was the most important oil source probably in the world at that point and there was oil refineries from many, many nations in Ploesti, and, in fact, Americano-Romano (ph) was one of the oil fields there and it was owned by an American company of some sort, some name. And around this concentration of oil wells, Hitler had a double railroad track put in and it was double tracked so that there could be two flack trains on there and they would circle the whole area so that regardless of what heading you came in to the target area, you were going to run through four layers of anti-aircraft, because they would get two as you approached it and two as you left the area, because you would still -- from bombs away until you really would dump the stick, you would be on that same heading, rather than screw up the formation. So you had four sets of flack cars to go through and it didn't depend on what heading -- or it had nothing to do with whatever heading you came in on; they could have those four trains on that heading, and it didn't take them long to establish what your heading would be. And in addition to that, they had the 105 anti-aircraft permanent implacements all over the area, which fired a bigger shell and was mainly aimed at the 24s who normally would fly 1,000 or maybe 2,000 feet higher than we were, and for that reason we were usually happy to know that there was 24s on the same mission, because the Germans knew that it was a fragile airplane compared to the fortress, which was certainly aptly named, and we could count on the curtain of flack being up above us if we happened to be on the same mission with B-24s. And I guess the best thing was once bombs away, the whole group would go into a shallow dive and close the bomb bays and start -- well, all along they would have manned the machine guns. And before I went overseas, the 17 had two cheek guns on the nose, which were to be manned by the navigator and the bombadeer. Well, with -- I think it was the G, the 17-G model, and maybe the model just before the G, they put on this chin turret, which the bombadeer could operate, and it was a swiveling turret with twin 50-caliber machine guns. They still kept the two cheek guns and the navigator would use those in defensive fire. So, in essence, we doubled the amount of arm or armament on the nose of the plane, which was, you know, the lead spot of the plane, and it was great fun. And I suppose I was an idiot, but I thought the greatest thing in the world was being behind the bomb site on take off and landing because it was such a thrill, really, to be out there ahead of the whole damn plane taking off or coming in, and you knew you were gonna be first in the air and first on the ground, really, and it was a thrill just to be there. And the navigators, I think, enjoyed it, too. One navigator that I flew several missions, he never wore his helmet on his head; he always sat on it. And I have no idea whether he ever got wounded or not, but I suppose there had to be hundreds of navigators who did the same thing, and maybe some bombadeers. But one thing that was a very natural growth of combat was that even though we had trained for weeks and weeks as a crew -- and we were formed into crews in Tampa, Florida at the center and then went out to phase training areas, and ours was in Avon Park, Florida. And when we had gotten our wings, we could put in for the kind of plane that we wanted to fly in combat, fly in, by the phase training center that we picked, and if you picked, I think it was Kansas City, you were going to go into B-24s. And when I heard that Tampa had the B-26 twin-engine and the B-17 four-engine, I said Tampa is where I want to go, and that's where I ended up and where pilots and engineers and navigators, all of the enlisted people, came from various training camps all over the country and would be formed into a nine or ten-man crew. And from there on you flew practice missions, each one practicing their own ability and their own training. And when we got over to a combat area, we found that this didn't work at all because you never would deliberately let a green crew go on a mission by itself so the navigator and the bombadeer would go with crews that were experienced. The copilot would fly as a copilot with an experienced pilot and the engineer would normally stay with the pilot. But the waste gunners and the tail gunner and the ball turret gunner and the radio man, they would fly sometimes with the copilot, but if they flew with the copilot then all of the other positions were veterans, and it was meant to avoid any casualties due to panic, which would certainly be a normal reaction to what happens on a bomb run, even though we were briefed repeatedly as to why it was so important when you're on a bomb run to concentrate exactly on what you were doing and don't worry about anything else, because all the rest of the ten-man crew were there to -- in essence, to see that the plane and yourself were protected in order to complete the mission.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Were you glad you got B-17s over B-26s?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Well, yes, in a way, because MacDill Field was right outside of Tampa, and one day while we were still at Tampa before we had been assigned to Avon Park, I went over to MacDill Field and they had a saying over there, "a plane a day in Tampa bay." (laughing) And the B-26 was a fabulous airplane, a twin-engine, and I thought for a long time during training that the Martin Marauder, which was the 26, that would be fitting for me to get into since it was my last name. Well, when I began to hear the difficulties -- because it was really built for maximum speed and it had, I would guess, a minimum amount of lift from its wings. And there were problems on occasion where if an engine sputtered you were likely to go in the drink, you know. And its missions would be shorter in duration as the B-25 Mitchell, which was a sort of a junior B-24. It was a twin-engine model and it was a more durable airplane than the 26, although the 26 was -- other than the A-20, which was a twin-engine fighter bomber that only had, I think, a three-man crew, and it was often used as low-level support. And it was a real rocket in those days. The A-20 was a -- and I don't know where the training ground was for that, I never -- but it was quite an amazing aircraft. And, anyway, I was happy that I got in the 17s. And when we finished our phase training, which would give everybody in the crew a definite time to perfect and smooth out their own performance, we had bombing runs out over the Caribbean and all along the east coast there and the Gulf. And the navigators would have to get us to a reading where we would have a bomb run and everybody would be practicing their own assignment, whether they were a ball turret or tail gunner or whatever. And then when we got through the hard work, we would have some play time getting back to the air field and they would let me fly the plane through crowds -- or clouds with the bomb site, and it was a relaxing way to get back home. And I remember in Italy a couple times when we were flying practice missions there, we would chase the Italian sheep all over, and, of course, the farmers didn't appreciate that, I'm sure. But after I had flown, I think, somewhere around ten missions, I had & R at the Isle of Capri, and that was where I met a lady who was a Red Cross executive or something and her duty was to see that the people who came to Capri on R&R were housed and fed and introduced to some of the historical parts of Capri. There were ruins of some of the Roman emperor's palaces, and one night I remember that we -- when several of us were invited to dinner at this lady's house, we were served octopus, which was the first time I think any of us had ever thought about eating octopus. We only eat the tentacles, and they're cut in, like, rings and you have to eat them very soon after they've been cooked or they get rubbery and it would be like eating a rubber band, actually. They didn't have that much flavor, but at least we ate them without any problem and it was a fun experience. And when I came back from there, I started to fly as a lead, and up until that time, I thought since I had, in the first two weeks, ten missions, I figured no time I'd be coming back to the states. In the meantime, I had heard from my sweetheart who had enlisted in the WAC and we were planning to get married as soon as I got back and I thought it would be by Christmas, but slowing down by only flying every fourth or fifth mission changed that schedule. And, anyway, she got an assignment at Wright Patterson Air Base, and during her time there she had arranged to sublet from an officer who was being transferred out. She figured when I got back and we got married and she was still on duty, we'd take over his apartment. And so when I did come back and we got married, we had to go down to Miami Beach for reassignment and when I got down there I was grounded permanently and couldn't serve as far north, actually, as Dayton. I had had rheumatic fever as a POW and lost a lot of weight, not only from that, but from the, more or less, rigorous calisthenics.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: You said your sweetheart sent you a picture overseas?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Yeah, and I had gotten that picture, actually, soon after she got in, and I think it was probably before I went overseas that I put that on a mirror and taped it. And the plastic that is all bubbled was perfectly flat, but I had it upstairs here in the attic one summer and the attic got so hot it just ballooned that piece of plastic, but it didn't hurt the picture itself. And it went with me on every mission that I flew and so I always -- I gave her credit for me being around.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Did you say that was on a metal plate?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Yeah, it was a reflective -- a stainless steel mirror, actually, which was part of an escape kit. And what I did was simply take it out of the canvas sleeve that it had and glued the picture to the front of it and wrapped the whole thing with a piece of clear plastic and wrapped the back of it with, I suppose, 10 or 15 layers of adhesive tape, because -- it was never questioned and never taken away from me. They looked at it and thought I was lucky, I guess, to have a sweetie in the uniform. And when I came back from overseas is when I cut the tape off the back of it, because to tell somebody that that had stopped a bullet fired, you know, right against my chest, if you didn't see the mirror, you would think you were dreaming. And this actually happened to be the piece of flack that caught me on the right wrist and my left thigh. It was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: So what about that bullet that was fired into you; when did that happen?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Oh, that was after I was captured -- in the process of being captured. This was on a mission before that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: But when you were captured somebody shot you?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Yeah. It was a single soldier who had been following me. And I've forgotten what he said to me, but I stopped and whatever I was carrying, I dropped and he bent down to pick it up and I jumped him. And in the wrestling around, he got his gun out against my chest and fired a shot. And I was able to break away and run, and I didn't run more than 50 or 60 yards at most because of having the heavy leather pants and boots, flying boots. It was not very easy to run in snow, and this was in February and the Alps were pretty deep in snow. And I had slept -- until I got to habitation on the third day, I guess it was, I had slept in my parachute wrapped up two nights. The first night, which would be the day of the mission, and the next day, because I walked those two days in the same direction with the aid of a compass so that I was able to get through the night all right. You could break pine boughs or branches of any kind to put down first and make a fairly good pad of your parachute and leave about half of it to pull over you and just curl up like a cocoon in it. For February and the first day of March, it was sleepable. I was glad that I had that kind of a uniform. Some of the bombadeers had opted for the electric suits and I, for some reason or other, didn't think an electric suit was that great. And, of course, if it got shot out you could freeze to death on a mission, and certainly if you landed in the snow that time of year in a silk flying suit that depended on electricity, you would hope to be captured pretty quickly or you would be in pretty serious trouble, because their winters are certainly just like ours or even worse. Anyway, that's how it happened, and then from there I went through -- had the --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: You were captured after a couple of days then?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: On the fourth day, I think. I walked two days, but -- let's see -- it took me two days to get to this house that I stayed overnight with, and it was late in the afternoon of the second day when I saw this little shed and a house and I walked up to the shed and went inside and it was a little storage barn for hay or whatever for the people's cow. And -- oh, I would guess no more than 15 minutes after I got in there, which was late in the afternoon, the doors opened and the man was there who obviously owned it, and he motioned for me to stay there and so I asked him for some water and he nodded but he said -- he made it plain that he wanted me me to stay inside because there were some other houses in the area and he didn't want anybody seeing that there was a stranger on his property. And after it got dark he came back and led me back to the house, which was maybe 150 yards, something like that. Had a couple children and his wife, and the first floor of the house was a stable. They had one cow and I've forgotten what else, but it seemed to me there was another animal there, and that was also storage for vegetables and whatever it was that was in that barn to feed the cow. And then you went up a flight of stairs to where the living area was and they had a wood-burning stove in the kitchen, which was the source of heat, and on the beds were these great big down -- like an enormous pillow, actually, and I slept that night with the man of the house under one of those things and it was completly warm; they're soft enough that they just come down around you. And about 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning the lady got up and whittled some kindling and made a fire in the stove, and we had had a warm dinner at night. And they got a girl who was a Finnish girl who lived next door to come over and she spoke a little bit of English -- or American, whatever. Anyway, the two of us could question and answer kind of thing and then she would tell them. She was actually married to a Wehrmacht soldier and he was on duty somewhere, but she had come back to this area because that's where the soldier was from and she lived in the house next door to these people. And so we talked through the evening about what I should do and where I should go from there and they went -- they all wanted to make certain that I was gone from their place before sunrise, or at least an hour before sunrise, so that they didn't get in trouble in case anybody saw me come out. And I would guess it would have been maybe 3:00 in the afternoon when I finally had this...meeting (laughing) with this German soldier who had been following me. Sometime around noon, as best as I could gauge, I had gotten to a little cluster of buildings and went into what apparently was a school, but it was completely empty and there was a funny looking kind of a toilet there and I had to relieve myself so I stayed in there, I suppose, maybe 10 or 15 minutes and then got zipped up and started walking again. And I would guess within a half an hour after that I could hear a dog's barking and -- although, the dogs never did show up, but apparently there was more than one person following me or following the footprints because the man that I had the disagreement with didn't have any dogs with him.

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: So after I had run a ways and then finally just ran out of gas, he took me to a little jail cell in a town pretty near to -- actually, it was within the -- I would say the same area where these houses were, and I spent at least one night there. And one of the two majors, I know, got out of the plane safely and to the ground safely because he had written his name on the wall, Major Alben (ph). And the bed was like a carpenter's bench, really, no mattress, and they had a little raised shelf for a pillow, and that was the bed. And I was there, I guess, a day and a night and the next morning, because the next morning I could hear formations outside and that particular little village of Fusen (ph) was also a training area for mountain troops. And I got up on this bench that I slept on, but I could not see out because the window -- the one window was still too high. But I could hear the marching feet and the commands so it was obviously some sort of a training area, and I asked eventually the man who came to take me from there and he said -- I think he said snow troops or something that made sense to me, but I never did see them. They were through their exercising before I ever got out of the cell. And we had a fairly long walk, and I remember that one time while I was still under personal escort, there was no other -- that we were somewhere during an air raid and he took me down into a shelter with a lot of civilians and that was an experience being on the other end, and it was like the basement of a department store or a subway station, something like that. And the trip then got broken down into different numbers of people and different -- when I finally got to Uber Ursel (ph), which was an interrogation center, you got sort of a cursory physical examination and you were housed inside a building in separate cells, which were not like jail cells with bars; they were closed rooms and a closed door. And it was made known to you that you were not to speak to anybody that you saw there other than a German who might be questioning you, so if you did see other POWs, it was not -- they wouldn't stand for you talking with them. And the repeated questioning section -- sessions, you know, name, rank and serial number and over and over and over again, and I think I was there two to three days with this ritual being carried on. And I remember having a physical examination at that point. And from there, then I became a part of a large group of prisoners; I would guess there was 75 to 100. And we had a -- we first had Wehrimarcht escorts, which was all right, except that once they were replaced with Luftwaffe personnel, we were more comfortable because there was a different attitude by the German air force toward the air force personnel. And we had been segregated at -- over Ursula (ph) into -- I think if there happened to be any ground troops they were separated from the rest of us, because we were made up of some Polish people, some Canadians, and Americans and English and we were all air force of one kind or another and once we got under the guidance and control of the air force, we were a lot more comfortable because they seemed to have a different attitude toward us than what the ground troops did. And we went to another interrogation center and eventually we got to -- we were supposed to get to a huge permanent prisoner of war camp outside of Normanburg, I think, and we got there and it had been evacuated. This was about noon time we got -- and we were on a sort of a hillside outside of the place after being marched up to it and finding out that it was completely deserted and we couldn't even get in. So we were back on the road marching again, and this had to be somewhere around noontime because the 8th Air Force then came over and bombed the hell out of the -- and then after they left we continued our march and they marched us right through the city, which was a dumb thing to do from our viewpoint, because there were a lot of civilians out fighting their own fires and some military personnel, and to walk you through a targeted area that had recently been a live target, you know, we were lucky to have as many escorts as we had because there were plenty of allies that got beaten up and killed with farm tools, whatever weapons that happened to be available, and I did hear about some being beaten to death with shovels, so in that respect we were well off to have a lot of escorts. And we had gotten to a small village, and I don't know what the name of it was, but we were going to have a ride in a train, a freight train, which was -- if you recognize our gondola cars, which have a low side, well, their gondola cars were open-top like ours, but the walls were about six feet high instead of three or four feet, and we had all been loaded into, I think -- I think there were two cars that we were gonna have, and there were somewhere around 100 people in the group. And we were -- oh, I would say no more than 20 minutes from getting out of there and a group -- a squadron of P-47s came by on no particular -- this certainly was not a target because this was a little town, not nearly as big as what Chagrin Falls would be. But it had a flack train on the railroad siding next to the one where our freight car was. And some idiot decided that he was gonna shoot down an allied plane and these 12 planes just went into a targeting circle and dropped their entire load of bombs in this little village and strafed the hell out of it. Well, when we realized what was going to happen because of this idiot, we left the two cars, and Major Alben, that I then had met, took part of them and they went into the village and beyond on one side. And the other group of guys went with me and we went across a huge meadow into a big drainage ditch, which was, I guess, maybe four feet deep, but at the top maybe 15 feet wide, and it was obviously something to control runoff from the meadows. And we -- there had to be 75 or 80 of us there and we got down in there and stayed there, and I would think that we were easily 150 to 200 yards from the railroad. Then we watched this whole process, and this one flack train and one gunner was certainly no match for the 12 P-47s, which were very heavily armed for ground support in addition to bombs. And when it was all over, why, we heard somebody -- well, we thought it was all over -- we heard somebody in a clump of bushes about two thirds of the way back to the village crying, and another guy -- I grabbed another fellow and we ran across the meadow to this clump of undergrowth and -- because this guy, whatever he was saying, he was screaming and that's all we knew. We got there and it was a German soldier and he had been hit in one foot by one of the 50 caliber projectiles. So we got him up on his good foot and carried him back into that ditch, and when we left he was still there, but some of the guards who had gone with us were seeing that he was going to be cared for. And we went back into the village and there had been a group of the political prisoners there who were not allowed to seek shelter during the raid, and as a result, there were five or six of them that had been wounded. And about the time that we were just looking at this mess, a guy came in on a motorcycle, a big, large man, and -- one of the S.S. storm troopers in a black leather uniform, put some of us together on one of these four-man hydraulic hand pumps to feed water into some of the places that were on fire. And then he went around and casually shot the political prisoners who were wounded and rounded up those who were not wounded to dig spots right there and bury them. And I guess that was the only time that I was actually abused, because I yelled at him or at somebody and one of the soldiers came over and knocked me down with a rifle butt, so I figured it was probably wise to keep my mouth shut at that point, because this guy was an absolute brute, and I think there were either five or six that had been wounded and he just calmly shot them and the other poor guys in those uniforms were put to digging holes and they were the most pitiful -- everywhere we saw them, and I remember on one train -- train ride that we had we passed through an area where they were working outside on something or other, whether they were being abused because we were going by in a train or whether it was just natural instance, it was really pitiful, and so many of these people were Germans who were educators and doctors and had been vocal in their resentment or their disagreement with Hitler, and as a result, they became the worst-treated prisoners in the -- in many ways, they were worse than the Jewish population because they were simply worked to death and fed starvation rations and really did get worked to death; there was no question about it. So it was a lesson for all of us to see that kind of brutality and know, you know, firsthand what was going on, even with some of the German people. And we never did get that train ride. From there on we started walkin' again, and I guess eventually we did get down to Stalag 7-A, which is at Musburg (ph). But on the way down there on one series of marches I had gotten very sick, a bad fever, and we did have a truck ride or a series of trucks that picked us up for a ride and I remember laying on the knees of three guys sitting on a -- the side board bench, and they kept me from falling off because I was pretty sick. And when we got to Musburg, to Stalag, I was put in a little infirmary. And it seems to me that I was there most of the time until -- well, I apparently did recover, because once I got out of the infirmary is when I made that little metal dish and was up and around and on foot when one of Patton's tank arms came through. I don't know how many tanks there were, but there was no conflict. The German prison force left during the night, and right along with the tanks coming in was a Red Cross truck, panel truck, with white bread and some crackers and some cookies and two gals driving it. These gals had just -- after what receptions we had back at Manperdonia (ph) in Italy where we were based, they never failed to be out there on the field when we came back and they were there to listen to anybody who had lost a friend or seen somebody wounded or whatever, you know, and so it was a remarkable experience to see them right with the land troops. And so then we had two or three days of just on our own and that's when we started roaming around, and I don't know who it was that found this little warehouse, but all of this stuff, including that dagger and a Walther pistol, that I did not take over to the school (laughing), that's where they all came from. And when we got to Camp Lucky Strike -- well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Did you make your own way back to the American lines, then?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Were you taken back by members of Patton's unit or did you make your own way?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Oh, no, there were trucks brought in, and I would guess they had to be—

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Took you over to Camp Lucky Strike?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Yeah, and we had a truck ride, and I'd guess maybe less than an hour from the camp to where they found a -- I would guess it was part of a farm or something and they mowed it off and we were put around the perimeter, because there were several thousand at Stalag 7-A. If you look at that picture in Brokaw's book, page 163, I think, is the picture of Stalag 7-A the day it was liberated and there are hundreds of people in that picture. And I showed the book -- well, I think it was my son that got me that book and then my youngest daughter looked at that picture with a magnifying glass and she said, "I think I see you." (laughing) Well, they're all -- you know, they're like these little spots here. But I've been meaning to write to Brokaw and just tell him that that particular picture taken that day was where I was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Sure. Now, you said that two of you bailed out, right?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Well, everybody had bailed out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Right, but you said the last two --

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Yeah, the last two.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: But what happened to the other guy; do you know?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: I've no idea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: He just landed somewhere else?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: I never actually saw anybody until sometime on the marching. Then I did see Major Alben, and I did know that he was alive, but -- because of his name on the wall, but none of the other people that were in that crew -- I have no idea what happened to them. In fact, I don't know what happened to the crew that I was originally part of, whether they finished their missions or not. I was the oldest -- the navigator and I were the oldest two on the crew, and he got killed in a really stupid accident. They were on a bomb run on a specific heading and altitude and another group of allied planes -- and I don't know whether they were English or what -- were on the same out -- heading, but 1,000 feet higher, and their bomb loads went right through our bomb group. And Tornay (ph), the navigator that I was -- part of my original crew was on one of the ships that got hit. By that time the bombs were armed and it just vaporized. And another guy that bailed out over Yugoslavia and walked to freedom, and apparently was welcomed by the Yugoslav forces and Tito's government, I suppose, came back to the air base and he wanted to fly one more mission or two, whatever. Anyway, he didn't have a flying suit and I had just put in for a knee-length parka with a hood on it and I had not actually flown a mission in it and I said -- and I think his name was Brian, a big, big fellow, bigger than I was, but this parka was big enough -- and he was a copilot and he wanted to fly another mission and he flew and he got fatally wounded on that mission with machine gun fire, apparently from a fighter. And when they came back, I never saw him, but I was told that the machine gun fire had cut the hood right off his parka. And it was the weirdest thing that some people who insisted on flying an extra mission when there were legally able to go home would do it, and almost without fail, something bad happened to them. Another officer that I knew who had finished wanted to fly a mission as a tail gunner and they -- from ground fire or fighter fire, their electrical system for the tail turret was shot out and both his hands froze and just -- it became so obvious that you shouldn't -- if you made your tour, don't trust lady luck, you know, to come again. It's just -- it was insanity because you -- if something like that happened, it just spread throughout the whole area. Everybody would know about it inside of this short time, you know. You didn't do that because you tempted fate and you lost. I don't know whether I got anything --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: We talked about Ploesti, but I don't think we talked about the other mission you had that was particularly bad.

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A. Oh, to Blechammer. Yeah, B-L-E-C-H-A-M-M-E-R. And I don't know what the target was except that it was to hell and gone it was such a long mission. And it was heavily defended, but it was not oil fields. I don't know what it was, but it was -- whatever in briefing we learned that that was going to be a target for the day. It was a mission that was going to have some losses to it because it was a well-defended -- and the fact that it was -- as I recall, it must have been very deep into either Poland or Czechoslovakia, because the deeper the mission, as far as length is concerned, the more possibilities of malfunction in the heating system or anything in the plane, you know, even though it was a miraculous aircraft, but the shorter the mission, the better the odds (laughing), to be frank about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Do you remember having any trouble adjusting after you got back?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Well, when I first came back, the first year at Pratt Institute in New York when I went to art school -- or when I came back, yeah. I drove a cab for a while in Warren and then I got to the point where some of the people as passengers really got on my nerves. In fact, I had to stop and let one guy out because he said I can't -- I can't stand your driving, and I had driven him almost to where he wanted to go so he got out and I got no fair, you know. But I went back down to Republic Steel where I had worked from getting out of high school. I had started driving an electric tractor in the hot strip section, and when I came back from service I was given a job in the Coke plant because it was a better income producer. The Coke plant runs 24 hours a day from the time it's built until it's torn down where the hot strip finishing and cold strip and bar mills, depending on the amount of orders, may be up or down, you know, on any particular week. And I had gotten -- Isabelle and I got married the 25th of August, and up until that time we had -- I had been going down to Dayton to see her whenever I could. And I guess that since I had been artistically blessed from the time I was in third or fourth grade, and my senior year in high school I didn't -- I had enough credits that I only took art classes, so a lot of people told me I should go to art school and I wrote to Pratt Institute, which was very well known, an excellent reputation, and took the home examination over a period of a couple of weeks. They would send different problems that you then had 48 hours or something like that to do it and send it back. And so I went back -- or went to Pratt, I think, in probably November of '46, something like that, and that first year at Pratt I had to go up to Cainesbridge (ph) Veterans Hospital in the Bronx once or twice a week because I no longer had a problem with the rheumatic -- at least I didn't know about it -- rheumatic fever. But I was having all kinds of arthritis problems with my legs and hands and feet and sometimes in my neck, and it was rheumatoid arthritis, and what happens is your joint becomes inflamed and it can be any place in the body for 24 hours and the next day it will be someplace else. And the worst would be if I'd get it at the base of my head and the base of my neck. And the first year is the more difficult, really, in an art school because it's a generalized education process, a lot of work, and after the first year then you specialize and your workload is definitely a particular category. But anyway, I would have enough problems with the rheumatoid arthritis that I went up to the Cainesbridge Hospital for heat treatments and massage and they told me that as long as I didn't take any more than 20 aspirins a day, that would be okay. And so it eventually wore off, and on occasion I have a flair-up, but it's nothing like it was that first year there, and that was especially difficult because it was our second year of marriage and we had our first daughter. And Isabelle got immediate discharge from the WAC when I was grounded.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Was the war still going on in Japan and the Pacific when you came back?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: You came back in May or something?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Yeah, there was still conflict over there and I don't know for sure when it actually --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Well, it's fortunate you were grounded, otherwise they would have probably tried to reassign you over there, right?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: Well, that's very likely, huh, and at that point the Super Fortress was being used over there and it's possible that, having finished a tour in Europe, that you could have been still assigned to --

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: -- and that would be a losing agenda as far as I'm concerned. If you got through -- just as I mentioned, you know, guys who had finished their allotted tour -- and it originally started out, I think, in the desert air force, if you flew 25 missions you got rehabbed or recirculated and then it went up to 50 when it became the European part of the war. And the two cases that I personally knew about who were free to go home -- and other people, apparently, from what I had heard in conversations later on had heard the same thing, you know, that knew somebody that decided to fly an extra mission. And more often than not it was somebody who was -- who was not a pilot, and in some cases some people who were not even air crews, who had a job on the ground, you know, and they thought it would really be a great adventure to fly. Well, it was as long as you got back, but the alternative is for the birds. (laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: You don't have (coughing) -- excuse me -- you don't have a defense against flack.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: And when you're in the bomb run you can't really --

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: -- do any evasive maneuvers?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: There's nothing you can do about it except hope that you get through it because there is no defensive mechanism against it where against fighter attacks you do have. But here -- this is what I was looking for -- this is what the sky looks like over a target. And those are all bursting either 88-millimeter or 105s.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: And in your position, you would see that up in front and you'd have to fly right through that and just hope?

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: That's right, yeah. And on any target, one of the things that happened that I got to take part in, after I came back from Capri, I was sent up to Rome, where the 15th Air Force headquarters were, and there was a special operation called Operation Pepper Pot and it was to be second and third class transportation centers over as much of Germany and Austria as we could cover. And these were low-level flights by B-17s at 500 feet and we had to use what was called a D-8, which was a mechanical bomb site, rather than the Sperry (ph) or Nordon (ph). And we went in in groups of three planes per target for little places like -- well, if Chagrin had a little crossroad intersection or a bridge or a bus station or a truck outlet, then we flew these missions three planes to a target at 500 feet. And the B-17s had never been done and, as far as I know, it was the only time it ever was done. And I don't know whether there were casualties or not. But we -- being up in the nose and flying in at that altitude was almost like you were flying through the tops of the trees. You were still safely above them, but -- somebody's brainstorm, and being only three planes to a target there was, you know, dozens and dozens of these secondary transportation centers that could be hit and put out of -- and certainly Hitler's ability to move around was greatly curtailed. Some of the marching we did was at night, and they were moving all kinds of equipment on the same roads that we were walking in the formation and sometimes we'd just pile into the ditches or whatever was alongside the road because truck and tank convoys at midnight, you know, are not going to be watching out for pedestrians, especially if -- if you're them other folk. (laughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert M. Martin
sp.p: A: But I remember one time that we -- we were marching somewhere near one of the cities and I forgot -- but they had taken 88-millimeter aircraft guns and brought them down like this and zeroed them in on a highway that we were on, which was apparently expected to be an invasion route by the allies, and these were hidden in undergrowth, you know, or big shrubs like we've got, and to walk up and be that close to the -- the muzzle of these damn things, you know, that in itself was a frightening experience. And walking through the city that was still on fire, that was just sheer madness, and I think it was -- there was no need to have marched us through the city after the British had pulverized it, pretty much. But I'm sure that some commander thought -- or that Collum (ph) thought it'd be a great idea.
